zh.summary: 先記住：先辨認要保護什麼、可能怎麼受損，再根據發生可能性與影響安排防護。發現弱點，不等於已經發生入侵。

sourceBody.text: Module 01：Introduction to Ethical Hacking（道德駭客入門）
本堂課的核心觀念：資訊安全不只是找出系統哪裡有問題，而是判斷什麼東西需要保護、可能遭遇什麼危害，以及應該優先解決哪些問題。
這四個概念是後續學習漏洞掃描（Vulnerability Scanning）、滲透測試（Penetration Testing）及風險管理（Risk Management）的基礎。
預計閱讀時間：8～10 分鐘。
本文的咖啡廳、醫院與 Northstar 都是合成教學情境，不是實際事件或第三方測試結果。
一、先用生活中的例子理解四個概念
假設你開了一間咖啡廳。
某天，你發現店裡的保險箱沒有上鎖。
這時候，我們可以問四個問題：

rows: 什麼事情可能造成損失？
哪裡存在安全上的不足？
可能發生損失的程度有多大？
現金被偷的可能性及損失金額

sourceBody.text: 這裡有一個非常重要的觀念：
發現保險箱沒有上鎖，不代表現金已經被偷走。
同樣地：

items: 發現伺服器有漏洞，不代表駭客已經入侵。
發現資料夾權限設定錯誤，不代表資料已經外洩。
發現系統使用過時的軟體，不代表系統一定會被攻擊成功。

sourceBody.text: 這就是資訊安全工作中，必須區分「已發現的弱點」與「已經發生的事件」的原因。
這些定義與美國國家標準暨技術研究院（NIST）的資訊安全術語及風險評估架構一致。[NIST：Asset](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/asset)
二、四個概念分別代表什麼？
1. Asset（資產）：我們要保護什麼？
很多初學者會以為，資訊安全所說的資產就是電腦、伺服器或網路設備。
實際上，資產不一定是實體物品。
例如，一間醫院可能具有下列資產：
因此，Asset 最重要的判斷標準是：
這項東西如果遺失、損壞、遭到竄改，或無法使用，會不會造成損失？
如果會，它就可能是值得保護的資產。
2. Threat（威脅）：什麼事情可能造成損害？
Threat 不一定是駭客。
例如：

items: 駭客嘗試竊取病歷。
員工不小心刪除資料。
機房發生火災。
停電導致醫院系統中斷。

sourceBody.text: 這些都可能構成威脅。
另外，必須區分兩個英文詞：
Threat Source（威脅來源）：可能造成危害的人、事物或條件。
Threat Event（威脅事件）：可能帶來不良後果的具體事件。
例如：
威脅來源是駭客，威脅事件是未經授權讀取病歷。
威脅來源也可能是自然災害，威脅事件則是淹水導致設備停止運作。
3. Vulnerability（弱點）：系統哪裡有不足？
Vulnerability 可以想成安全防護中的缺口。
例如：
技術上的弱點：

items: 系統沒有安裝必要的安全更新。
使用容易被猜到的密碼。
資料庫權限設定錯誤。

sourceBody.text: 管理上的弱點：

items: 離職員工的帳號沒有停用。
沒有適當的權限審查流程。
員工缺乏必要的資安訓練。

sourceBody.text: 要特別注意：
弱點不一定來自程式漏洞（Software Vulnerability），也可能來自錯誤設定或管理流程。
NIST 的定義同樣包含系統、程序與內部控制上的弱點。[NIST：Vulnerability](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/vulnerability)
4. Risk（風險）：這個問題有多值得擔心？
現在假設我們發現兩個問題：
A：醫院網站的公開活動照片資料夾權限設定錯誤。
B：醫院的私人病歷資料夾權限設定錯誤。
兩者都可能是弱點，但造成的損失可能非常不同。
如果 B 的資料能被不應存取的人讀取，就可能造成嚴重的個資外洩。
因此，不能只計算發現多少個弱點，還必須評估其實際情境與後果。
風險評估通常考慮兩個關鍵因素：
Risk ≈ Likelihood × Impact
其中：

items: Likelihood（發生可能性）：事件有多可能發生並造成損害？
Impact（影響程度）：如果發生，後果有多嚴重？

sourceBody.text: 這是一個幫助初學者理解的簡化模型，不代表所有風險都能用兩個數字精確相乘。NIST SP 800-30 也強調威脅來源、弱點、既有防護與事件後果等因素。[NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/final)

visual.caption: 風險要回到情境比較
visual.description: 補充圖解｜相同權限錯誤，不代表風險相同。公開資料也要保護完整性與可用性。

items.title: 公開衛教文章
items.body: 可公開閱讀；若遭竄改或刪除，仍可能傷害讀者或中斷服務。

items.title: 私人病歷資料
items.body: 不應公開閱讀；未授權揭露可能影響隱私與病患信任。

items.title: 共同判斷條件
items.body: 誰能做什麼、接觸機會、既有防護、可能後果；不能只數弱點。

sourceBody.text: 用途與條件：盤點、修補排序或審查權限前，先確認系統範圍、資料用途、正常使用者與評估期間。
三、把四個概念串成一個完整流程
我們用虛構的 Northstar 教材平台來練習。
情境：
Northstar 是一間線上教育公司。
它的系統保存學生的個人作答資料，原本只有學生本人與老師可以閱讀。
但是，管理員不小心把資料夾的分享設定改成：
「任何取得連結的人都可以閱讀。」
現在應該如何分析？
第一步：辨認資產
學生的私人作答資料就是 Asset。
我們希望保護這些資料的機密性（Confidentiality）。
第二步：辨認威脅事件
可能有不應取得資料的人，透過分享連結閱讀學生的作答。
這是 Threat Event。
第三步：找出弱點
資料夾共享權限設定錯誤。
這是 Vulnerability。
第四步：評估風險
需要調查：

items: 1. 取得連結有多容易？
2. 連結是否曾公開傳播？
3. 資料包含哪些敏感內容？
4. 是否有其他存取限制？
5. 資料外洩可能造成什麼損害？

sourceBody.text: 掌握這些資訊，才能合理評估 Risk。
第五步：採取防護措施
例如：

items: 修正資料夾的分享權限。
使用不同權限的測試帳號進行驗證。
確認學生與老師仍可正常使用。
檢查適當的存取紀錄。

sourceBody.text: 這些措施稱為 Security Controls（安全控制措施）。
整個流程可以整理為：

① Asset
   辨認需要保護的資產
       ↓
② Threat
   辨認可能發生的危害
       ↓
③ Vulnerability
   檢查有哪些弱點
       ↓
④ Risk Assessment
   評估發生可能性與影響
       ↓
⑤ Security Controls
   採取適當防護措施
       ↓
⑥ Residual Risk
   評估防護後仍存在的風險
這是一個入門分析流程，而非所有風險情境都必須依照這個順序發生。
特別提醒，修正弱點不代表風險一定歸零。
例如，管理員雖然修正了分享權限，但無法僅憑這個動作確認先前的資料沒有被複製。
採取控制措施後仍然存在的風險，就稱為 Residual Risk（殘餘風險）。[NIST：Residual Risk](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/residual_risk)
四、CEH 考試最容易混淆的三組觀念

rows: 威脅是可能造成危害的情況或事件；弱點是可能被利用或觸發的不足。
弱點描述哪裡存在問題；風險評估問題可能造成的損害及其可能性。
發現弱點，不代表已經發生資安事件。

sourceBody.text: 這裡再補充一個重要觀念。
假設系統管理員發現一台伺服器存在高嚴重性的軟體漏洞。
我們能直接判定這台伺服器對組織構成最高風險嗎？
不能。
還要考慮伺服器是否暴露於外部網路、是否有防護措施、是否保存重要資料，以及漏洞是否容易在實際環境中被利用。
因此：
漏洞嚴重程度（Severity）不等於組織的實際風險（Risk）。
這個差異會在 CEH M05「Vulnerability Analysis（弱點分析）」繼續使用。
五、建立資訊安全人員的證據觀念
請記住三個層次：
Observation（觀察）
我們發現私人資料夾允許任何取得連結的人閱讀。
Inference（推論）
這個設定可能讓未經授權的人取得資料。
Verification（驗證）
我們透過授權的測試帳號，確認不同身分是否真的能讀取資料，並檢查相關紀錄。
如果目前沒有找到未授權存取的紀錄，應該怎麼理解？
這只能表示：
「目前尚未找到足以證明未授權存取的紀錄。」
它不等於已經證明事件從未發生。
原因是系統可能沒有完整保留存取紀錄，或某些資料存取方式沒有被記錄。
對資安工作而言，知道什麼已被證實、什麼只是合理推測，以及什麼仍然未知，是非常重要的能力。

visual.caption: 從觀察到可支持的結論
visual.description: 補充圖解｜三個層次不是三個自動成立的結論。每一步都要交代證據與限制。

items.title: 觀察 Observation
items.body: 設定顯示：取得連結的人可讀取。

items.title: 推論 Inference
items.body: 這可能造成未授權揭露，尚不等於已發生。

items.title: 驗證 Verification
items.body: 授權測試確認實際權限；日誌查核支持事件判讀，但缺紀錄不是沒事件。

sourceBody.text: 六、本堂課重點整理
今天先掌握四句話：

items: 1. Asset：我們要保護什麼？
2. Threat：什麼事情可能傷害它？
3. Vulnerability：哪裡有可能被利用或觸發的弱點？
4. Risk：這件事情發生並造成損害的可能性及後果有多大？

sourceBody.text: 記憶口訣：
「保護什麼 → 怕什麼 → 弱在哪裡 → 有多危險」。
學習 CEH 時，這四個概念不只是考試名詞，也能幫助我們理解後續每一個資安技術到底要解決什麼問題。
七、理解測驗（先試答，再展開參考解答）
假設一家醫院發現，某個存放病患資料的資料夾被錯誤設定成「所有院內員工都能閱讀」。
目前尚未找到未經授權閱讀資料的證據。
問題一：概念辨認
請指出：

items: A. 這個情境中的 Asset 是什麼？
B. Vulnerability 是什麼？
C. 可能的 Threat Event 是什麼？
D. 能不能直接宣稱病患資料已經遭到竊取？為什麼？

sourceBody.text: 問題二：風險判斷
現在有兩個系統：

items: 系統 A：存放公開的衛教宣導文章。
系統 B：存放病患的完整個人病歷。

sourceBody.text: 兩個系統都有相同的資料夾權限設定錯誤。
請問：
兩者的風險一定相同嗎？為什麼？
你可以直接回答 A～D 及問題二。我會依照你的答案，檢查你是否真正理解這四個概念，並針對需要補強的地方進一步說明。
頁面展開答案只供自己核對，不會把作答送出，也不代表已經理解；仍需由你實際回答後再確認理解狀態。

sourceBody.summary: 展開問題一參考解答｜資產、弱點、威脅事件與證據
paragraphs: A. 資產是病患資料。重點不是只有那個資料夾，而是裡面需要保護的個人資訊與病歷。
B. 弱點是權限開得太大：所有院內員工都能讀，沒有依照工作需要限制誰可以看。員工身分不代表有權看每一位病患的資料。
C. 可能的威脅事件是：沒有業務需要或未獲授權的員工，讀取或複製病患資料。這是可能發生的事，目前不代表已經發生。
D. 不能直接說資料已被竊取。我們目前知道的是權限設定有問題；要說有人真的看過或帶走資料，還需要其他證據。可以在授權範圍內，用測試帳號核對存取權限，並查閱相關日誌。
找不到紀錄，也不能反過來保證沒有人看過，因為日誌可能不完整。最準確的說法是：已確認權限過寬，尚未找到足以證明未授權存取的證據。

sourceBody.summary: 展開問題二參考解答｜相同弱點，不一定是相同風險
paragraphs: 不一定。權限設定錯誤相同，只能說弱點類型相同；風險還要看資料、實際能做的操作、接觸機會、防護與後果。
完整病歷涉及敏感個資，因此在其他條件相近的情況下，被不該看的人讀取，通常會造成較大的機密性與隱私損害。
公開衛教文章本來就供人閱讀，但不代表完全沒風險。如果錯誤權限還允許修改或刪除，文章被改成錯誤健康資訊，或網站無法使用，也可能造成嚴重影響。
所以不要只看漏洞名稱或嚴重性分數。先問：誰能做什麼、可能造成什麼損害、現有防護是否有效，再比較風險。這裡沒有足夠資料算出精確的數字。

en.summary: First identify what needs protection and how it could be harmed, then prioritize defenses using likelihood and impact. Finding a vulnerability does not mean an intrusion has occurred.

sourceBody.text: Module 01: Introduction to Ethical Hacking
Core idea: information security is not only finding faults in systems. It means deciding what needs protection, what could harm it, and which problems deserve attention first.
These four concepts underpin vulnerability scanning, penetration testing and risk management.
Estimated reading time: 8–10 minutes.
The café, hospital and Northstar examples are synthetic teaching scenarios, not reports of actual incidents or tests against third parties.
1. Understand the four concepts through everyday life
Imagine that you run a café.
One day, you discover that the safe is unlocked.
We can ask four questions:

rows: How significant is the possible loss?
The likelihood of theft and the amount lost

sourceBody.text: A very important distinction:
Finding an unlocked safe does not mean the cash has already been stolen.
Likewise:

items: Finding a server vulnerability does not mean an attacker has already broken in.
Finding incorrect folder permissions does not mean data has already leaked.
Finding outdated software does not mean an attack will necessarily succeed.

sourceBody.text: This is why security work separates a discovered weakness from an incident that has actually occurred.
These definitions align with the terminology and risk-assessment framework of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). [NIST: Asset](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/asset)
2. What does each concept mean?
1. Asset: what are we protecting?
Beginners sometimes think security assets are only computers, servers or network equipment.
An asset need not be a physical object.
A hospital, for example, may have these assets:
The key question for identifying an asset is:
Would losing, damaging, altering or being unable to use it cause harm?
If so, it may be an asset worth protecting.
2. Threat: what could cause harm?
A threat is not necessarily a hacker.
Examples include:

items: An attacker attempting to steal medical records.
An employee accidentally deleting data.
A fire in the equipment room.
A power outage interrupting hospital systems.

sourceBody.text: All can constitute threats.
Also distinguish two terms:
Threat source: a person, thing or condition that could cause harm.
Threat event: a particular event that could produce adverse consequences.
For example:
An attacker is a threat source; unauthorized reading of medical records is a threat event.
A natural disaster can also be a source, while flooding that stops equipment is the event.
3. Vulnerability: where is protection inadequate?
Think of a vulnerability as a gap in protection.
Examples:
Technical weaknesses:

items: Missing necessary security updates.
Easily guessed passwords.
Incorrect database permissions.

sourceBody.text: Management weaknesses:

items: Accounts of former employees remain active.
No appropriate access-review process.
Staff lack necessary security training.

sourceBody.text: Remember:
A vulnerability need not be a software flaw; it may come from misconfiguration or a management process.
NIST's definitions also include weaknesses in systems, procedures and internal controls. [NIST: Vulnerability](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/vulnerability)
4. Risk: how concerned should we be?
Suppose we discover two problems:
A: incorrect permissions on a hospital website folder containing public event photographs.
B: incorrect permissions on a folder containing private medical records.
Both may be weaknesses, but their consequences can be very different.
If people who should not have access can read B, serious disclosure of personal information could result.
Counting weaknesses is therefore insufficient: assess the actual context and consequences.
Risk assessment commonly considers two key factors:
Risk ≈ Likelihood × Impact
Where:

items: Likelihood: how likely is the event to occur and cause harm?
Impact: how serious would the consequences be?

sourceBody.text: This is a simplified learning model, not a claim that all risk can be precisely calculated by multiplying two numbers. NIST SP 800-30 also considers threat sources, vulnerabilities, existing safeguards and event consequences. [NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/final)

visual.caption: Compare risk in context
visual.description: Supplement: the same permission error does not imply equal risk. Public information also needs integrity and availability.

items.title: Public health articles
items.body: Intended for public reading; alteration or deletion can still harm readers or interrupt service.

items.title: Private medical records
items.body: Not intended for public reading; unauthorized disclosure can harm privacy and trust.

items.title: Shared assessment factors
items.body: Allowed operations, exposure, safeguards and consequences—not merely a weakness count.

sourceBody.text: Use and conditions: before inventorying systems, prioritizing patches or reviewing permissions, define the system boundary, data purpose, normal users and assessment period.
3. Connect the concepts into a complete process
Practice with the fictional Northstar learning platform.
Scenario:
Northstar is an online education company.
It stores students' private answers, intended to be readable only by the student and teacher.
An administrator accidentally changes the folder's sharing setting to:
“Anyone with the link can read.”
How should we analyze this?
Step 1: identify the asset
The students' private answers are the asset.
We want to protect their confidentiality.
Step 2: identify the threat event
Someone who should not have access might use the sharing link to read the answers.
That is the threat event.
Step 3: identify the weakness
The folder's sharing permissions are incorrect.
That is the vulnerability.
Step 4: assess the risk
Investigate:

items: 1. How easy is it to obtain the link?
2. Has the link been shared publicly?
3. What sensitive information does the data contain?
4. Are there other access restrictions?
5. What harm could disclosure cause?

sourceBody.text: This information supports a defensible risk assessment.
Step 5: apply safeguards
For example:

items: Correct the folder's sharing permissions.
Verify with authorized test accounts having different permissions.
Confirm that students and teachers can still use the service normally.
Review appropriate access records.

sourceBody.text: These measures are called security controls.
The process can be summarized as:

① Asset
   Identify what needs protection
       ↓
② Threat
   Identify possible harm
       ↓
③ Vulnerability
   Identify weaknesses
       ↓
④ Risk Assessment
   Assess likelihood and impact
       ↓
⑤ Security Controls
   Apply appropriate safeguards
       ↓
⑥ Residual Risk
   Assess risk remaining after safeguards
This is an introductory analysis process, not a mandatory chronological order for every risk scenario.
Remember: fixing a vulnerability does not necessarily reduce risk to zero.
Correcting sharing permissions alone cannot establish that no one previously copied the data.
Risk remaining after controls are applied is called residual risk. [NIST: Residual Risk](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/residual_risk)
4. Three distinctions that are easy to confuse

rows: A threat is a circumstance or event that could cause harm; a vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited or triggered.
A vulnerability identifies a weakness; risk considers possible harm and its likelihood.
Finding a vulnerability does not establish that an incident has occurred.

sourceBody.text: One more important point:
Suppose an administrator finds a high-severity software vulnerability on a server.
Can we immediately conclude that this server poses the organization's highest risk?
No.
We must also consider internet exposure, safeguards, important data and whether exploitation is feasible in the actual environment.
Therefore:
Vulnerability severity is not the same as the organization's actual risk.
This distinction returns in CEH M05, Vulnerability Analysis.
5. Develop an evidence-based security mindset
Keep three levels separate:
Observation
We find that a private folder allows anyone with the link to read it.
Inference
This setting could let unauthorized people obtain the data.
Verification
Using authorized test accounts, we check whether different identities can actually read the data and inspect relevant records.
How should we interpret finding no unauthorized-access records?
It only means:
“We have not yet found records sufficient to establish unauthorized access.”
It does not prove that the event never occurred.
The system might not retain complete access logs, or some forms of access might not be recorded.
Knowing what is established, what is a reasonable inference and what remains unknown is an essential security skill.

visual.caption: From observation to supported conclusions
visual.description: Supplement: these are not three automatically established conclusions. Explain evidence and limits at every level.

items.title: Observation
items.body: The configuration permits anyone with the link to read.

items.title: Inference
items.body: Unauthorized disclosure is possible, not yet established.

items.title: Verification
items.body: Authorized tests check permissions; logs support incident analysis, but missing records do not prove no incident.

sourceBody.text: 6. Key takeaways
Remember four questions:

items: 1. Asset: what are we protecting?
2. Threat: what could harm it?
3. Vulnerability: what weakness could be exploited or triggered?
4. Risk: how likely is harmful occurrence, and how serious are its consequences?

sourceBody.text: Memory aid:
“What matters → what could harm it → where is the weakness → how significant is the risk?”
These are not merely exam terms: they help explain the problems that later security techniques address.
7. Understanding check: try first, then reveal the reference answers
A hospital discovers that a folder containing patient information is mistakenly readable by all hospital employees.
No evidence of unauthorized reading has yet been found.
Question 1: identify the concepts
Identify:

items: A. What is the asset?
B. What is the vulnerability?
C. What is a possible threat event?
D. Can we claim that patient data has already been stolen? Why?

sourceBody.text: Question 2: assess risk
Consider two systems:

items: System A stores public health-education articles.
System B stores patients' complete personal medical records.

sourceBody.text: Both have the same folder-permission error.
Question:
Must their risks be identical? Why?
You can answer A–D and Question 2. Your explanation can then be reviewed for understanding and any topics needing reinforcement.
Revealing an answer is only a self-check. It does not submit a response or establish understanding; that requires reviewing your actual explanation.

sourceBody.summary: Reveal Question 1 reference answer: concepts and evidence
paragraphs: A. The asset is patient information, not merely the folder holding it.
B. Permissions are too broad: all employees can read the data instead of access being limited by work needs. Being an employee does not authorize access to every patient record.
C. A possible threat event is an employee without a legitimate need or authorization reading or copying patient information. Possible does not mean observed.
D. No. Incorrect permissions establish a weakness, not that someone actually read or stole the data. Within authorized scope, use test accounts to verify permissions and inspect relevant logs.
Missing records do not prove absence of access, because logs may be incomplete. Report that excessive permissions are confirmed while evidence establishing unauthorized access has not yet been found.

sourceBody.summary: Reveal Question 2 reference answer: same weakness, different risk
paragraphs: Not necessarily. The same permission error identifies a similar weakness, while risk also depends on data, allowed operations, exposure, controls and consequences.
Complete medical records contain sensitive personal information. Other things being equal, unauthorized reading would usually have more serious confidentiality and privacy consequences.

Public health articles are intended to be read, but that does not mean zero risk. If erroneous permissions also permit modification or deletion, false health advice or unavailable content could cause serious harm.

Ask who can do what, what harm could result and whether safeguards are effective. A vulnerability label or severity score is not enough, and this scenario does not support an exact numeric risk calculation.
